We need to propose a retrosynthesis route (max 3 steps) to target SMILES: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2)cc1

Let's parse: It's a para-methyl phenyl sulfonamide attached to another phenyl ring bearing a trans-α,β-unsaturated amide (C= C - C(=O)N- phenyl-NH). So overall: 4-(methyl) phenyl-sulfonyl attached to para phenyl with a cinnamamide (trans). Also the amide has an aniline (NH) attached to phenyl.

We need to break into commercially available precursors within 3 steps.

Potential disconnections:

1. Disconnection of sulfonamide: break S-N bond to give sulfonyl chloride (or sulfonic acid) and aniline. So we could start from p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (TsCl) and the aniline (the other phenyl with the cinnamamide). The target has sulfonamide linking the two aromatic rings: the sulfonyl attached to the first phenyl (p-tolyl) and the nitrogen attached to the second phenyl (the one bearing the cinnamamide). So we can form sulfonamide by reacting p-toluenesulfonyl chloride with the aniline (the second phenyl with amide). So step 1: sulfonamide formation.

Thus precursors: p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (commercial) and 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline? Wait the second phenyl is substituted with the amide side chain at para position relative to the sulfonamide? Let's examine SMILES: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2)cc1

We have first phenyl (ring A) with methyl at position 1 (para? Actually "Cc1ccc(... )cc1" indicates methyl at position 1, sulfonamide at position 4 (para). So ring A is p-tolyl-sulfonamide.

The sulfonamide nitrogen attached to S(=O)2 attached to ring B (c2ccc(... )cc2). So ring B is phenyl with para substituent being the trans-cinnamamide (C= C - C(=O)N- phenyl-NH). The amide attaches to phenyl (c3ccccc3N) which is an aniline (para? Actually the amide nitrogen attached to phenyl with an NH substituent (aniline). So the amide is N-phenyl- (i.e., anilide) with an NH on that phenyl (i.e., an aniline). So the amide is -C(=O)N-Ph-NH2 (para? Not specified). The SMILES: Nc3ccccc3N indicates an aniline with an NH2 at the same carbon as the amide? Actually "Nc3ccccc3N" means an aniline where the nitrogen attached to carbonyl is attached to aromatic carbon (position 1) and there is another NH attached to the same aromatic carbon? Wait "Nc3ccccc3N" is an aniline with an NH attached to the aromatic carbon (the first N is attached to carbonyl, the second N is attached to aromatic carbon as substituent? Actually "Nc3ccccc3N" means N attached to aromatic carbon (c3...), and that aromatic carbon also has an N attached (the trailing N). So it's a phenyl with two amino substituents at same carbon? That seems unrealistic. Let's parse: "C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N" means carbonyl attached to N (amide), which is attached to aromatic carbon c3... The aromatic ring has an N attached at the end (the trailing N) meaning an aniline (para? Actually the N after the ring indicates an amine attached to the aromatic carbon at position 1 (the same carbon as the amide N). So the ring is an aniline where the amide nitrogen is attached to the aromatic carbon, and there is an NH2 substituent at the same carbon? That would be a diamino phenyl? Might be misinterpretation; maybe the SMILES is "C(=O)N c3ccccc3 N" meaning the amide nitrogen attached to phenyl, and that phenyl has an NH2 substituent at para position (the trailing N after the ring). But SMILES would need a position indicator like "c3ccc(N)cc3". So "c3ccccc3N" is an aniline (aniline is "c1ccc(cc1)N"). So "c3ccccc3N" is phenyl with NH2 at position 1 (attached to the aromatic carbon). So the amide nitrogen attaches to the phenyl carbon (position 1) which also has NH2? That would be N attached to carbon that also has N? Not possible. So maybe the SMILES is "C(=O)N c3ccccc3 N" meaning the amide nitrogen attached to phenyl, and the phenyl has an NH2 substituent at para? Actually the SMILES for para-aminobenzamide would be "O=C(Nc1ccc(N)cc1)". That's "O=C(Nc1ccc(N)cc1)". Our SMILES: "/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N" missing aromatic positions. So it's likely "C(=O)N c3ccccc3 N" meaning anilide with an aniline substituent at para? Not sure.

Nevertheless, we can treat the amide side chain as derived from trans-cinnamic acid (or trans-3-phenylacrylic acid) and an aniline (para-aminophenyl?). Actually trans-cinnamic acid is C6H5-CH=CH-COOH. If we couple with an aniline (p-aminophenyl) we get an amide: C6H5-CH=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2 (para-aminophenyl). So the second phenyl (c3ccccc3N) is an aniline (para? not defined). So we can propose to make the amide via amide coupling of trans-cinnamic acid (or its activated derivative) with p-aminophenyl (aniline). That is step 2.

Thus overall retrosynthesis:

Target -> disconnection 1: sulfonamide formation between p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (TsCl) and intermediate B (the aniline with cinnamamide). So step 1: sulfonamide formation.

Intermediate B: 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline? Actually the sulfonamide nitrogen attaches to the phenyl ring B at para position relative to the cinnamamide substituent. So B is a phenyl bearing para-cinnamoylamide and para-sulfonamide? Wait the sulfonamide attaches at the nitrogen, not carbon. So B is an aniline (NH) attached to sulfonyl group; the aromatic ring B has the cinnamamide substituent at para position relative to the sulfonamide nitrogen (since the SMILES: c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2) indicates the phenyl ring B has the cinnamoyl amide at para position (since the substituent is at position 1 of the ring, and the sulfonamide attaches at the nitrogen, not carbon). Actually the sulfonamide nitrogen attaches to the sulfonyl group, not to the aromatic carbon. So the phenyl B is attached to the sulfonyl via the nitrogen (i.e., sulfonamide N attached to S). So the phenyl B is attached to the sulfonyl via N, not via carbon. So B is an aniline (NH) that is sulfonylated (forming sulfonamide). So B is 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline (para-cinnamoyl aniline). So we can get B by sulfonylating p-aminophenyl with TsCl? Wait we need B as the aniline (with cinnamoyl) that will be sulfonylated. So B = 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline (para-aminophenyl with amide at para). This can be synthesized by amide coupling of trans-cinnamic acid with p-phenylenediamine (or 4-aminophenylamine). Actually we need an aniline with two amino groups: one for sulfonylation (the one that becomes sulfonamide) and one for amide formation (the one that becomes amide). The SMILES shows the phenyl B has an amide attached via nitrogen (C(=O)N-Ph-NH2). So the phenyl B has an NH2 group (the aniline) that is attached to the carbonyl (amide). The sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the sulfonyl group, not to the phenyl B carbon. So the phenyl B is attached to the sulfonyl via its nitrogen (the same nitrogen that is part of the amide? Wait the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the sulfonyl and to the phenyl B carbon? Actually sulfonamide is R-SO2-NR' where N is attached to sulfonyl and to R' (which is phenyl B). So the phenyl B is attached to the nitrogen, not via its own nitrogen. So phenyl B is a phenyl group attached to the sulfonamide nitrogen (i.e., N-aryl sulfonamide). So the phenyl B does not have an NH group attached to it; the nitrogen is attached to the phenyl carbon (aryl). So the phenyl B is a phenyl ring attached to the sulfonamide nitrogen (aryl sulfonamide). The phenyl B also has a para substituent: /C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N (cinnamamide). So the phenyl B is a phenyl with a para cinnamamide substituent, and the nitrogen of the sulfonamide is attached to the phenyl B carbon (aryl). So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the phenyl B carbon (aryl) and to the sulfonyl group. So the phenyl B does not have an NH group; the amide is attached to the phenyl B carbon via carbonyl to an aniline (c3ccccc3N). So the amide is attached to phenyl B via carbonyl to an aniline (para-aminophenyl). So the amide side chain is: phenyl B -CH=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2 (aniline). So the amide nitrogen is attached to an aniline (c3ccccc3N). So the aniline is separate.

Thus the target can be assembled by:

- Step A: Form sulfonamide between p-toluenesulfonyl chloride and phenyl B (aryl amine). Wait phenyl B is not an amine; it's an aryl group attached to nitrogen (aryl sulfonamide). To form aryl sulfonamide, we need an aniline (aryl amine) reacting with TsCl to give aryl sulfonamide. So phenyl B must be an aniline (i.e., p-aminophenyl) that after sulfonylation becomes aryl sulfonamide. However phenyl B is attached to sulfonamide nitrogen, not carbon. So the aryl sulfonamide is formed from aniline (p-aminophenyl) where the nitrogen is attached to sulfonyl. So phenyl B is an aniline (p-aminophenyl) that after sulfonylation becomes N-aryl sulfonamide. So the phenyl B must have an NH2 group (aniline) that will be sulfonylated. In the target, the nitrogen is attached to sulfonyl and to phenyl B carbon (aryl). So yes phenyl B is an aniline (Ar-NH-). After sulfonylation, we get Ar-NH-SO2-Ar' (where Ar' is p-tolyl). So phenyl B must be 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline (para-cinnamoyl aniline). That is an aniline with a para substituent being the cinnamoyl amide.

Thus retrosynthesis:

Target -> disconnection of sulfonamide: separate into p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (commercial) and 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline (intermediate I).

Intermediate I -> disconnection of amide: separate into trans-cinnamic acid (commercial) and p-phenylenediamine (or 4-aminophenylamine). Actually we need an aniline with para amino group to attach cinnamoyl at para position. Starting from p-phenylenediamine (1,4-diaminobenzene) we can acylate one amino group with trans-cinnamic acid to give 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline. Then sulfonylate the other amino group with TsCl to give target.

Thus steps:

1. Amide coupling: trans-cinnamic acid + p-phenylenediamine (selective acylation of one amine) -> 4-(cinnamoylamino)aniline (intermediate I). Could use standard coupling reagents (e.g., DCC, EDC). This is step 1.

2. Sulfonylation: p-toluenesulfonyl chloride + intermediate I (the remaining free amine) -> target sulfonamide.

That's only 2 steps (plus maybe protection to ensure selectivity). But we can assume chemoselective acylation of one amine is feasible.

All precursors: p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (TsCl), trans-cinnamic acid, p-phenylenediamine. All are commercially available and cheap (<$100 each). So total cost well under $9999.

Now we need to produce JSON route with up to 3 steps. The format: root node is target molecule (type mol, smiles). Children are reaction nodes with template_id (we need to provide template IDs). We need to find appropriate template IDs for sulfonamide formation and amide coupling.

We can search for templates for sulfonamide formation (aryl amine + sulfonyl chloride). Use search_template_catalog_by_criteria with functional_groups_formed = ["sulfonamides"] and maybe bonds formed: S-N. Let's try.
